newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan near decision on whether to break up NTT.
newsitem.headline: Japan near decision on whether to break up NTT.

text.p: An agreement could be reached soon in the long-running debate over whether to break up Japanese telecoms giant Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), the company and the government said on Monday.
A possible breakup of NTT, which at present enjoys a monopoly over Japan's local telephone networks, has been mulled for more than a decade.
The government argues that a breakup is needed before letting NTT enter global telecommunications markets.
Financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Monday that the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications and NTT had reached a compromise deal on a new structure for the company.
Under the agreement, it said, a holding company would be set up to control three units of NTT -- a long-distance operator and two regional firms -- by the end of March 1999.

A ministry official said the ministry was seeking an early conclusion on a possible NTT breakup, but declined to confirm the report. "We hope to reach an agreement as soon as possible on a plan to break up the company, but we haven't set any specific deadline," the official told Reuters.
A NTT spokesman said an agreement was expected in December.
"Although an agreement is expected to be reached this month, it is too early to say this is one," the spokesman said when asked about the newspaper report.

The Tokyo stock market responded positively to the report by boosting NTT shares to 830,000 yen ($7,345) at the opening, up 18,000 yen ($159) from Friday's close. By early afternoon it had slipped back to 814,000 yen ($7,203).

"There was some thinking in the market that a breakup may be a negative factor for NTT, but the reports today said it would become a long-distance operator, which means it will become more competitive internationally, and that provided the share price with support," said Masayuki Matsumoto, an analyst at Dai-ichi Securities.
A ministry panel proposed in February that NTT, which holds 80 percent of Japan's domestic telecoms market, be broken up.

But the government, which owns 65 percent of NTT, postponed a decision on whether to split it up until next year, after some members of the then-ruling coalition opposed the breakup, saying it could erode NTT's competitiveness.
NTT has opposed being split into smaller firms, saying it would weaken its research and development base amid increasingly competitive global markets.
The planned mega-merger of British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp of the United States has also brought to the surface fears that NTT may be lagging behind its foreign rivals.

The idea of creating a holding company to control the smaller NTT units could be seen as a compromise which would halt any decline in the NTT's research and development ability after a breakup, the newspaper said.
The newspaper reported that under the plan, current shareholders of NTT would become shareholders of a holding company to be set up to control the smaller NTT units.
But for that plan to take effect, the government must clear another major hurdle by lifting a nearly 50-year-old ban on the setting up holding companies.
Earlier this year, the three parties in the then-ruling coalition failed to come up with an agreement on how to revise the anti-monopoly law banning holding companies.
The paper also said government bodies and NTT would enter negotiations this week to set details of NTT's new structure.

The ministry will submit a bill to revise a law limiting NTT to domestic services during a regular parliamentary session to be convened in January, paving the way for NTT to get an international long-distance licence, it added. ($1=113 yen)
